**Verdict:** No. Paul Graham would tell you not to start a startup while you're in college. He would also tell you to keep building the side project. If it takes off on its own, with real users pulling it forward, then you have a real choice, and he says it may be reasonable to run with it, even though that would mean dropping out.

**Based on:** something he said directly, in 2014 to Stanford students, and repeated with a different emphasis in an August 2026 essay.

**Why he'd say it**
- **You can't be a student and a founder at once.** "you can't start up a startup as a student, because if you start a startup you're not a student anymore." ([Before the Startup, 2014](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1102s) @ 18:22). In 2026 he still holds it: "Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student." ([How Universities Should Prepare Founders](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
- **20 isn't the best age, and waiting costs you nothing.** "Do not start a startup in college." … "20 is not the optimal time to do it." (@ [18:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s)). He also says "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." (@ 21:12)
- **Your early twenties are for exploring, and success would end that.** He says to "plunge deeply into projects on a whim that seem like they have no payoff" (@ 19:32). His example is Zuckerberg: "Facebook is running him as much as he is running Facebook." (@ 20:40)
- **The exception is your situation.** If a side project takes off by itself the way Facebook did, "Then you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." (@ 21:12)

**How his view shifted by 2026:** he kept the rule, but now stresses the exception. He wants universities to give students more free time because "a significant number of those side projects would be incipient startups." He points out that Microsoft and Meta both started during Harvard's reading period. Once one takes off, he says the student has to choose: "abandon them? Because it's either that or drop out." He doesn't say which to pick.

**Related views of his:**
- He retracted his old advice to work at a company first. Now he says "the best way to learn how to start a startup is to try and start it" (@ 33:36). So when you graduate, he'd want you to start one, not take a job first.
- In [Superlinear Returns (2023)](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html) he says risky, high-variance paths suit "particularly the young, who can afford to risk trying it to find out." He also says to start taking risks early.

**What would change his answer:** whether the project is pulling you forward or you're pushing it. "Should I turn my side project into a startup?" gets a no. "My side project is growing faster than I can keep up with while in school" is the Facebook case, where he'd say running with it may be reasonable.

**Verdict:** Yes, but you don't have to stay. In April 2026 Paul Graham gave a talk in Stockholm on exactly this question, and his answer was that you should go to Silicon Valley at least for a while, and ideally come back.

> "Should I go there? And the answer is the same now as it always is. Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." ([talk @ 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s))

**Based on:** something he said directly. This is the only talk on location in the vault, and he said it to a Stockholm audience, so it fits your case closely.

**Why he says it**
- **Every field has one center, and ambitious people should go to it.** His examples are Paris for painting, Göttingen for math and Hollywood for movies. Crossing a national border doesn't change that: "that doesn't change when you're moving across a dotted line on a map" ([@ 1:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=69s)).
- **Better peers, and more of them.** "The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them" ([@ 1:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=69s)). You get more chance meetings that turn out to matter ([@ 2:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=134s)), and things move faster because people "egg one another on" ([@ 3:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=233s)).
- **Investors.** "Investors outside Silicon Valley implicitly assume that any local startup is second rate. It's not a uniquely Swedish problem." If you go, "you make this rule operate in reverse. You automatically rise in investors' opinion" ([@ 6:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=399s)). Valley investors also decide faster, because competition means good deals don't wait.
- **What it does to you.** He calls this the biggest effect: "not what it does for you, but what it does to you" ([@ 8:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=499s)). "When you're a big fish in a small pond, you don't even know how big a fish you are" ([@ 8:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=532s)). Seeing the successful founders up close makes the goal look "no longer… impossible… just a hard one" ([@ 10:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=634s)).
- **Going and coming back helps Stockholm too.** "As long as you do actually come back, that's one of the best things you can do to help Sweden to help Stockholm thrive as a startup hub" ([@ 16:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=970s)). You bring back a better startup, US investors' money and the Valley's culture. He adds that Stockholm "could make it the Silicon Valley of Europe. That job is still up for grabs" ([@ 20:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1204s)).

**What he recommends doing:** go through YC. "Surely the optimal way to go to Silicon Valley for a bit and then come back is to do YC" ([@ 17:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1036s)). He admits this sounds like he's "talking my own book."

**The cost of going home:** He says YC startups that return home after the program are "only about half as likely to become unicorns." He discounts the figure himself, because it also reflects "the confidence and the determination of the founders" who choose to stay ([@ 18:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1137s)). He also notes that money isn't everything: "Once you have kids, you'll find you care more about them than your company" ([@ 19:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1170s)).

**What would change his answer:** In this talk, nothing changes the "at least go" part. The only open question he leaves is whether you stay, and he treats that as a choice about your life, not a mistake.

**Caveats:**
- He's YC's founder, telling founders to come to YC. He points out the conflict of interest himself.
- Sam Altman, in July 2026, agrees but less firmly. He thinks "move to the Bay Area" is probably still good advice but says he has "less of an intuition for it now" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38)).

I've read the YC vault's fundraising pages and Seibel's thinking page, and I have enough to answer.

**Verdict:** Seibel would tell you to stop. Months of pitching, deck polishing and follow-up meetings that don't close is the trap he fell into at Justin.tv. Put that time into making the company one investors chase. Fundraising gets easy when the business is working, not when the deck is better.

**Based on:** he said it (October 2026 episode with Dalton Caldwell, plus his 2019 MVP talk). Applying it to your situation follows from his rules, with high confidence.

**Why he'd say it**

- **He has lived your situation.** He spent about eight months trying to raise for Justin.tv. With two months of runway left, the team switched to making it profitable. He says they got more done in those two months than in all the months of pitching:
  - "we got to figure out how to make this thing profitable or we're going to die." ([7TU636F_yVQ @ 6:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s))
  - "if you just think about how much time is wasted, it's like a it's like a drag on the industry." (same, @ 6:44)
- **Make yourself a company investors chase. Don't decksmith.** Investors told him they chase 80–90% of their deals. Only 10–20% come through the front door, where you're pitching from now.
  - "if you can invest that time in making your company something that investors will chase after versus decksmithing, you're you're playing into the odds versus playing out of the odds." ([7TU636F_yVQ @ 10:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=603s))
  - When Socialcam was the #2 app in the App Store, the deck barely mattered: "one of our pitch decks kind of just was like here's some questions you can ask us." (@ [9:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=570s))
  - Back in 2019 he made the same point: "spending all that time on a pitch deck is not as valuable as spending your time building anything that you can give to a customer." ([1hHMwLxN6EM @ 11:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=671s))
- **Endless follow-ups mean you have no leverage.** In that episode, Seibel and Caldwell say VCs mostly invest on traction. An investor who keeps taking meetings is holding a free option in case you take off, and the meetings make that less likely. Leverage means being able to walk away, and you build it before the negotiation through growth, not with tactics in the room. The vault doesn't attribute these lines to either host by name, so I'm paraphrasing. ([[why-investors-string-founders-along]], [[building-leverage-before-negotiating]])
- **His sales rule applies to investors too.** Don't wait on the one deal you want. Keep filling the funnel, because "if you're a customer, you don't like to feel that the company you're considering needs you more than you need them." ([7TU636F_yVQ @ 13:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=836s)) Reading this as advice about investors is my inference, not something he said about them.

**What he'd have you do instead** (follows from his rules)
1. Set a hard deadline for the raise and stop taking follow-ups that have no clear path to a check.
2. Spend the time on users, revenue and growth. If you haven't launched, launch something rough now. His definition: "launch is when you get any customers." ([1hHMwLxN6EM @ 10:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=607s))
3. Plan as if the money won't come: cut burn and look for a path to profitability, the way Justin.tv did.
4. Raise again once your growth makes investors come to you.

**What would change his answer:** if you already have strong traction and still can't close, the problem isn't the deck or your effort. Then he'd point you to his line that investors' "no" isn't a verdict. Brian Armstrong got the demo day signal that investors didn't want to give him money: "if he had taken the demo day signal the investor signal of oh we don't want to give you money and quit we don't have coinbase" ([Jcuqq48CNj8 @ 12:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=723s)). Even then the advice is to keep building, not keep polishing.

**Caveat:** the October 2026 fundraising episode is co-hosted by Caldwell, a partner at Standard Capital, which sponsors the show. So the "respect founders' time" message also promotes his fund. The core advice that traction beats pitching matches what PG said in 2014.

**Verdict:** Seibel would tell you to stop the lawyer letters. Agree on a no-fault split, ask your cofounder to give back most of his stock even though it has vested, and finish it in about a week for about $2,000. At 9 months, he'd put your cofounder's stake at 1–2% of the company or less.

His reasoning is that before product-market fit the stock is worth nothing, so a legal fight over it is really a fight over ego, and it can leave you in debt. Nearly all the value is still to be created by whoever stays, so that's where the equity should go.

**Based on:** he said it. He addresses almost exactly your situation in *Dalton + Michael*, "Do You Need a Co-Founder for Your Startup?" (2026-07-13), https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U

**Why he'd say it**
- **On lawyers:** "in a situation where you're having a co-founder breakup and the stock is worth nothing, paying lawyers a bunch of money makes no sense." ([@ 11:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=696s)) He also says "a lawyer can suck up infinite amount of your ... anger and monetize it." ([@ 12:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=727s)) He habitually asks whose business model a choice feeds, and a letter-trading war feeds the lawyers'.
- **On vested stock:** "even if you vested, like get down to under 5% of the company, if it's within the first year, under 2%." ([@ 18:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1119s)) Later in the same episode he puts the first-year figure at "1%, 2%, sometimes less than 1%." ([@ 21:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1282s))
- **On why the leaver should give it back:** "the vast majority of the value this company could create hasn't been created yet" ([@ 14:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=887s)), and "you get to hedge. The founder staying doesn't." ([@ 15:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=921s))
- **On how to close it:** "Do reasonable severance, sign clean paperwork and and peace out", and "you could do that whole thing in a week and spend like $2,000." ([@ 18:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1119s))
- **On how the founder who stays should behave:** be generous and act as the responsible party. "it is so cheap to be nice" ([@ 17:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1053s)), and acting that way means "often you don't trigger victimness on the other side, too." ([@ 18:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1086s))
- **On blame:** "If you made a list of all the things we screwed up in our company, it would be way longer than the things you're pissed at your co-founder about." ([@ 21:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1314s))
- **On mediators:** "If you're using someone to mediate this, don't make them the judge." ([@ 19:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1186s)) His co-host Dalton Caldwell adds: "the facts don't matter," so build a go-forward plan instead of arguing over who was right.

**What he's done:** When a cofounder leaves, he says he often talks to the departing founder first and makes the case for leaving the equity with the team that stays. YC also has written breakup standards, so both cofounders get the same advice.

**In practice:** One of you should pick up the phone, outside the lawyers. Propose a split with no fault on either side: he keeps a small stake (1–2% or less), gets reasonable severance, and you both sign simple paperwork. If he won't budge, bring in a neutral party, such as an investor or advisor you both trust, to help you reach a deal rather than rule on who's right.

**What would change his answer:**
- Misconduct. He says "if your co-founder is breaking the law, doing something unethical, killing people, none of this applies." ([@ 21:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1314s))
- Real traction. The advice assumes the stock is worthless before product-market fit. If the company has real value, the stakes change.

**Caveats:**
- The percentages are rules of thumb, and his figure for the first year shifts slightly within the episode.
- Some of these quotes are matched to Seibel by following the flow of the conversation, not a clear speaker change. That gives them medium confidence. The lines at 20:50 and later are certainly his.
- The episode is sponsored by Standard Capital, the Series A fund Caldwell co-founded.

My own note: his numbers are something you ask your cofounder to accept, not something you can force. Vested shares legally belong to him, so the only way to get them back is if he agrees. Before you sign anything, have one lawyer check the final paperwork.

Garry Tan didn't say this. It was Sam Altman, speaking at YC's Startup School in July 2026, and he made a point of saying it was something Tan couldn't say himself.

**Verdict:** Altman says the YC premium has grown because of network effects. As more of the people you'll eventually start companies with pass through YC, joining it gets you into that network faster than anything else does.

**Based on:** something said in the vault, by Altman, with Tan's response in the same session.

**What Altman actually said** ([Sam Altman: "Never a Better Time to Do a Startup"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s), 2026-07-28):
- "I also think that I I can say this, Gary probably can't. I I I think the premium on doing YC is bigger now than it's like ever been before. Uh, the distance between like YC and second place is has expanded. And this is a reminder of the power of network effects." (@ 16:56–17:28)

**His reasoning, from the surrounding passage:**
1. **Finding co-founders is the real bottleneck.** He says that five or ten years earlier, the main limit on how many good startups YC could fund was "figuring out how to solve the co-founder matching problem." (@ 16:25)
2. **Networks compound over time.** He met the people he started OpenAI with "many many years in some cases before" founding it. So "the sooner you can put yourself just in a flow where you're going to meet the people that will be your eventual co-founders… the better." (@ 17:28) His example: he met Greg Brockman by helping Stripe recruit him, and about eight years later they co-founded OpenAI together. (@ 18:35)
3. **YC is now the strongest such network.** The old advice was to move to the Bay Area, where "magic happened… lucky chances and collisions." He still thinks that's "probably good advice," but says he has "less of an intuition for it now." (@ 16:56) He was more sure about the YC premium than about the Bay Area.

**Tan's part:** He didn't make the claim. He did back the reasoning behind it, saying that "this is the kind of like loose network and the spirit of helping each other and this like very long-term outlook has been an awesome thing" ([@ 23:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1415s)). He also told the room that someone there would meet a future co-founder (@ 23:03).

**Caveat:** Altman is YC's former president and said this at a YC event. His "Gary probably can't" admits the conflict of interest. No figures or comparisons with other accelerators back the "second place" claim; it's his assertion, not data.

**Verdict:** The vault doesn't support that premise. It shows Livingston saying close to the opposite. She did use "aggressive" and "ruthless" in her 2018 talk, but she was describing other **investors**, and she set herself against them. The founders she screened for were earnest, determined and flexible-minded, and she turned down anyone she saw as conceited.

**Based on:** said it (two Livingston talks, 2018 and 2024)

**Where the words actually come from**
In her 2018 talk "9 Things She Learned From Founding YC" (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1064s) she says:
> "I was soft and sensitive at a time when investors tended to be hardened and aggressive and I'll throw in ruthless - for a couple of them that I know" (@ 17:44)

She calls this "probably the thing that was most different about YC" and says it "felt like a family and I was its mom." She then talks about checking whether founders were overwhelmed or eating properly, and helping them through co-founder disputes. So she's describing the VCs YC set out to be different from, not the founders it funded.

**What she actually screened for**
- "did they seem earnest did they seem determined were they flexible minded and most importantly what was the relationship between the co-founders like" (2018 @ 14:51, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s)
- "from the beginning I was very careful about only funding earnest people" (2018 @ 14:51)
- She turned away applicants she could tell were conceited. She admits YC has funded some since, but says "early on I was pretty rigid about this and I think that's the basis of the culture of our alumni community" (2018 @ 15:27)
- "Earnest and not pretentious that's in YC's DNA" (2024, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=2734s)
- She tells founders to pick a co-founder with "the same moral compass as you" (2018 @ 23:59)

**What's close to the claim, and why it's still different**
- **Determination and boldness:** She does want founders who are tough. "You do need a certain amount of boldness to work on ideas that most people would consider stupid and to keep going when you're ridiculed or ignored" (2018 @ 25:45). In 2024 she said of the founders she'd known, "they're all very determined." That's persistence in the face of rejection, not being ruthless with people.
- **"Formidable":** Paul Graham, not Livingston, says YC wants "formidable" founders. He says the word comes from his and Jessica's private language, and his definition is "someone who gets what they want in any situation." He gives an investor's reason: "If they get what they want, you get what you want" (Sept 2026, yt-5bxp78i96S8 @ 9:57). That's probably the nearest thing to the quote you heard, but it's PG's, and it's about effectiveness, not ruthlessness.

**What would change this answer:** a Livingston source outside this vault where she praises ruthless founders. I didn't find one in either of her talks here, and her one use of "ruthless" is the investor line above. If you have a specific quote, send it and I'll check it against the raw transcripts.
